chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
On February 22, 2024, a six-legged lander named Odysseus touched down near the lunar south pole, became the first privately built spacecraft to land on the Moon, and announced the arrival of Intuitive Machines as something more than a NASA subcontractor with ambitions. The company had not gone public two years earlier with a particularly tidy story — a de-SPAC through Inflection Point Acquisition Corp in February 2023, a lumpy milestone-revenue accounting model, and the inherent operational risk of landing hardware on an airless body 238,000 miles away. But Odysseus changed the framing entirely.

## Company in Brief

Intuitive Machines (LUNR, NASDAQ) is headquartered in Houston, Texas, and was co-founded in 2013 by Stephen Altemus, who serves as Chief Executive Officer and President, and Dr. Kamal Ghaffarian, who serves as Chairman. Altemus came to the company directly from NASA Johnson Space Center, where he had served as Deputy Director and, in the aftermath of the February 2003 Columbia disaster, as Columbia Reconstruction Director — arguably the most operationally demanding aerospace-management role in the modern history of American human spaceflight. Ghaffarian, by the time Intuitive Machines was founded, had already built and sold Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies (subsequently acquired by KBR) and was simultaneously founding or chairing Axiom Space, X Energy, Quantum Space, and PTX. The founder-pair's NASA-institutional-credibility anchor and serial-entrepreneur capital-formation capability defined the company's early character.

The company's core product is the Nova-C class lunar lander, a vehicle designed to deliver scientific instruments, technology demonstrations, and commercial payloads to the lunar surface under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services program. NASA awarded Intuitive Machines a CLPS contract with a ceiling of $4.82 billion, with $150 million in near-term guaranteed value. The company is also developing the larger, cargo-class Nova-D lander; the $180.4 million IM-5 task order — the largest single CLPS award to date — calls for a Nova-D delivery to the Lunar South Pole.

## Financial Snapshot

Intuitive Machines' FY2025 financials reflected the inherent lumpiness of NASA milestone-payment revenue recognition. Fourth-quarter 2025 revenue came in at $44.8 million, down approximately 18 percent year-on-year, as IM-1 mission revenue had been substantially recognised in FY2024 and the company was in active preparation for subsequent missions. Full-year FY2025 revenue fell in the $250–$300 million range, with a Q4 gross margin of 19 percent — a workable figure for a capital-intensive aerospace developer, but not one that signalled operating-profitability inflection.

The inflection, management guided, was coming in FY2026. The company issued a revenue outlook of $900 million to $1 billion for the fiscal year ending December 2026, with positive Adjusted EBITDA — implying roughly 3–4x year-on-year revenue growth. Total backlog, post-Lanteris, stood at $943 million.

| Metric | FY2025 | FY2026 Outlook |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $250–300M | $900M–$1B |
| Q4 Gross Margin | 19% | — |
| Adj. EBITDA | Negative | Positive |
| Backlog | — | $943M (post-Lanteris) |

The dominant driver of that growth was a single transaction: the $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems, structured as $450 million cash and $350 million in stock, with an expected Q1 2026 close. Lanteris, led by Chris Johnson — previously President of Boeing Satellite Systems International — brought Boeing-pedigree satellite systems capability into the Intuitive Machines portfolio. Johnson assumed the title of President of Lanteris Space Systems within the combined company. The acquisition's strategic logic was explicit: Intuitive Machines was transforming from a lunar logistics specialist into a full space prime contractor with the satellite systems capability to compete for the broadest category of civil and national-security space programmes.

## Board and Governance

The six-director board that oversaw this transformation was unusually credentialled for a small-cap space company. Ghaffarian and Altemus anchored it as co-founders. William Liquori, a retired Lieutenant General and former Chief Strategy and Resourcing Officer of the U.S. Space Force, supplied the Pentagon procurement signal. Robert Masson — U.S. Naval Academy, Harvard MBA, ex-Raytheon CFO, Naval Aviator — chaired the Audit Committee. Michael Blitzer, founder of Kingstown Capital and the original Inflection Point SPAC sponsor who brought LUNR public, chaired Strategic Transactions, the committee that approved the Lanteris deal. Nicole Seligman — Harvard College and Harvard Law School both magna cum laude, former President of Sony Entertainment and Sony Corporation of America, former Global General Counsel of Sony Corporation, former clerk to Justice Thurgood Marshall, and a sitting OpenAI board director — provided corporate-governance credentialling of a depth rarely seen at a company of LUNR's market capitalisation.

## Central Tension

The company that presented itself to investors in the spring of 2026 had demonstrated lunar-landing capability twice — IM-1's Odysseus in February 2024 and IM-2's Athena in Q1 2025, both of which reached the lunar surface with operational complications but completed their primary mission objectives. It was executing the largest acquisition in its history. It was guiding to near-decadal revenue growth in a single fiscal year. Three questions remained open: whether the NASA Artemis programme would sustain the lunar economy thesis through the late 2020s at a pace sufficient to justify the CLPS contract ceiling; whether the Lanteris integration would deliver the space-prime-contractor positioning its price tag demanded; and whether IM-3, IM-4, and IM-5 would execute cleanly enough to validate the operational-execution model the entire investment case depended upon.

chapters.title: From JSC engineering office to NASDAQ space prime
chapters.body:
## The man who rebuilt Columbia

Stephen Altemus joined NASA in 1989, starting at Kennedy Space Center before moving to Johnson Space Center in Houston, where he would spend the better part of a decade working in the Engineering Directorate's Aeroscience and Flight Mechanics Division. He had earned a Bachelor of Science in Aeronautical Engineering from Embry Riddle Aeronautical University and a Master's in Engineering Management from the University of Central Florida — a pedigree that placed him among the technicians who made NASA's human spaceflight program run. He was not yet the public face of anything.

On February 1, 2003, the Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry over Texas and Louisiana, killing all seven crew members. The loss triggered one of the most exhaustive accident investigations and physical reconstruction efforts in aerospace history. Altemus was assigned as Columbia Reconstruction Director — the engineer responsible for organising the recovery of debris across 2.3 million acres and leading the technical reconstruction that would help investigators determine what had failed. It was a role that required institutional discipline, the ability to manage hundreds of people under sustained public and political scrutiny, and a capacity to hold enormous operational complexity without flinching. It remains, in the language of aerospace, one of the most demanding engineering management assignments of the modern era.

He was subsequently appointed Director of Engineering at JSC, and later Deputy Director of the entire centre — the second-ranking operational position at the institution that manages human spaceflight for the United States government. When he left NASA in 2013 to co-found Intuitive Machines, he carried with him not only a technical record but a set of institutional relationships across the agency that very few private-sector executives could replicate.

## A thesis about what NASA would become

The founding thesis, in 2013, was structural rather than speculative. Altemus co-founded the company in Houston with Dr. Kamal Ghaffarian, a serial deep-tech entrepreneur whose career had already produced Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies — a technical services firm that KBR would acquire in 2018 — and would go on to include co-founding Axiom Space, X Energy, Quantum Space, and PTX. Ghaffarian brought the entrepreneurial architecture and the capital-formation relationships; Altemus brought the NASA institutional credibility and the engineering rigour. Together, they made a bet that NASA's exploration mandate was shifting from agency-owned execution toward commercial procurement — and that a Houston-based aerospace company with deep JSC roots could be the private partner of choice for lunar logistics and deep space.

The thesis took five years to receive its first institutional validation. In 2018, NASA selected Intuitive Machines as one of the initial participants in the Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme — the procurement vehicle through which the agency intended to buy lunar delivery as a service rather than build the capability itself. The CLPS award gave Intuitive Machines a formal channel for what it had been building toward. Through 2019 to 2023, the company developed the Nova-C lander platform, a vehicle class designed to deliver up to 100 kilograms of NASA and commercial payloads to the lunar surface. It was an era of engineering development on a very long timeline, funded by NASA milestones and private capital, without any of the quarterly reporting obligations that would soon arrive.

## The SPAC window and the public listing

In February 2023, Intuitive Machines completed its business combination with Inflection Point Acquisition Corp., the special-purpose acquisition company sponsored by Michael Blitzer's Inflection Point organisation. Blitzer was the founder of Kingstown Capital Management, a multi-billion-dollar asset manager, and had built Inflection Point as a SPAC vehicle specifically oriented toward technology and innovation businesses. He joined the board of Intuitive Machines concurrent with the de-SPAC, in the role that would eventually chair the Strategic Transactions Committee — the committee that would later approve the $800 million Lanteris acquisition.

The company began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker LUNR. The board that assembled alongside the listing reflected a deliberate configuration: Dr. Ghaffarian as Chairman (Class III), Altemus as CEO and director (Class III), William Liquori as a Class I director carrying the credential of a retired Lieutenant General and Chief Strategy and Resourcing Officer of the United States Space Force, and Robert Masson as Class I director and Audit Committee Chair — a Naval Aviator turned CFO whose career had run through Raytheon, Flowserve, and Hypertherm with a Harvard Business School MBA as its foundation. In June 2023, the company appointed Nicole Seligman — former President of Sony Entertainment, former EVP and Global General Counsel of Sony Corporation, a Harvard Law magna cum laude graduate who had clerked for Justice Thurgood Marshall and was then serving as an OpenAI board director — as a Class II director.

The board that emerged was, by any measure, overqualified for a company at that revenue scale. It was also precisely calibrated for what Intuitive Machines needed: deep national-security procurement relationships, aerospace-finance rigour, and corporate-governance depth sufficient to manage a company navigating the intersection of NASA contract law, public-market expectations, and a genuinely novel operating environment.

## Odysseus lands on the Moon

On February 15, 2024, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted the Nova-C IM-1 lander — named *Odysseus* — from Kennedy Space Center. Seven days later, on February 22, *Odysseus* touched down near the Malapert A crater at the lunar south pole, becoming the first privately-built spacecraft to successfully land on the Moon and the first US-built spacecraft to soft-land on the lunar surface since Apollo 17 in December 1972. It was the moment the founding thesis, eleven years after Altemus and Ghaffarian registered the company in Houston, received its clearest physical proof.

The landing came with operational complications. A failure of the landing legs caused *Odysseus* to come to rest on its side, partially obscuring the solar panels and compressing the mission timeline. The lander nonetheless transmitted data and demonstrated that commercial lunar landing was a viable, repeatable capability rather than a theoretical one. In the early months of 2025, the IM-2 mission — *Athena* — launched carrying additional NASA and commercial payloads, reached the lunar surface, and encountered similar operational difficulties. Two missions, two lunar landings, two sets of lessons about the genuine difficulty of precision surface operations at 384,000 kilometres.

## Building the executive team for scale

As *Odysseus* was completing its mission in early 2024, the company was also reshaping its executive team for the transition from development-stage operator to operating-scale contractor. In September 2024, Peter McGrath joined as Chief Financial Officer, stepping into the role from his position as Vice President of Business Development at Intuitive Machines. McGrath had spent 31 years at Boeing, across structural analysis, Phantom Works, and launch services — a career that gave him both the engineering economics literacy and the large-programme financial management experience that a company approaching $300 million in annual revenue and a $4.82 billion NASA contract ceiling required.

The CLPS ceiling expansion itself, completed through 2024 and 2025, was a significant signal. NASA raised the total contract ceiling to $4.82 billion, with $150 million in guaranteed near-term task orders across the programme. The $180.4 million IM-5 task order — the largest single CLPS award to date, directing seven science and technology payloads to the Lunar South Pole aboard the larger cargo-class Nova-D lander — confirmed that Intuitive Machines was not merely one of several CLPS participants but was emerging as the programme's primary operational contractor.

## The Lanteris transaction and the identity shift

The single most consequential event in the company's history arrived with the announcement of the $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems — $450 million in cash and $350 million in stock, with an expected close in the first quarter of 2026. Chris Johnson, who had served as CEO of Lanteris and before that as President of Boeing Satellite Systems International, was named President of Lanteris Space Systems within Intuitive Machines effective January 2026. The acquisition brought Boeing-grade satellite systems product lines into a company that had built its identity entirely around lunar delivery. Total backlog post-Lanteris rose to $943 million.

The executive realignment of February 2026 formalised the new structure: Dr. Timothy Crain, the co-founder who had engineered the Nova-C lander platform after a NASA JSC career that spanned Mars Science Lander navigation and Orion spacecraft guidance systems, became Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. Anna Jones — a Northwestern Law JD whose career had run through Latham and Watkins, ConocoPhillips, Marathon Oil, and Paysafe — became Senior Vice President, Chief Legal Officer, and Corporate Secretary.

## What the arc means

At the frozen snapshot of May 23, 2026, Intuitive Machines had guided FY2026 revenue of $900 million to $1 billion — three to four times the FY2025 base — with positive Adjusted EBITDA. The shape of the company that Altemus and Ghaffarian founded in a Houston office in 2013, incorporated the credential of a man who rebuilt a destroyed Space Shuttle and the entrepreneurial capital of a serial deep-tech founder, is now something qualitatively different from what it was when *Odysseus* lifted off in February 2024.

The thirteen years from founding to a billion-dollar revenue outlook trace one of the more unusual arcs in the post-commercial-space era: a company that survived the SPAC cycle with its institutional credibility intact, executed two lunar landings before its competition reached the launchpad, and used the operational proof points from those missions to justify a transformational acquisition that repositions it as a full space prime. The Columbia Reconstruction Director credential that Altemus carried out of JSC in 2013 was never merely biographical colour. It was the institutional signal — to NASA, to the Pentagon, to the aerospace primes — that the people running Intuitive Machines had operated at the hardest end of the business before they ever asked anyone to trust them with a commercial lunar lander.

chapters.title: Lunar landers, NASA CLPS, and the satellite-systems pivot
chapters.body:
## Three lines, one mission

When Intuitive Machines filed its first annual report as a public company, it described itself in terms that its Houston founding team had spent a decade making credible: a commercial lunar delivery operator. By the time that description appeared in print, however, the company had already begun assembling the infrastructure to be something considerably larger.

The business as it stood through most of fiscal 2025 comprised three distinct revenue lines. Lunar Access Services was the flagship — the Nova-C and Nova-D lander programmes, flown under task orders issued through NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme. Lunar Data Services encompassed the company's proprietary telemetry, tracking, and command capability for in-space operations, a ground-system asset that could eventually become a standalone commercial offering. Orbital Services covered the broader space-systems engineering work that kept engineers and cash flowing between major mission milestones. Together, the three segments produced between $250 million and $300 million in fiscal 2025 revenue, according to figures disclosed in the company's [FY2025 10-K filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm). A fourth segment — satellite systems — was acquired rather than built, and its arrival in the first quarter of 2026 remade the company's financial profile entirely.

## Nova-C: the vehicle that made history

The Nova-C lander is a hexagonal carbon-fibre structure roughly the size of a compact car, designed to deliver approximately 100 kilograms of payload to the lunar surface. Intuitive Machines designed and built the platform at its Houston facility — propulsion, avionics, and software developed in-house, a degree of vertical integration unusual for a company at its scale. The lander burns liquid oxygen and liquid methane, propellants chosen in part for their compatibility with NASA's longer-term Artemis architecture.

IM-1, carrying the call sign *Odysseus*, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 on 15 February 2024 and touched down near the Malapert A crater on 22 February, becoming the first privately operated spacecraft to land on the Moon. The mission was not without drama: a software misconfiguration disabled the lander's laser rangefinders before descent, forcing the crew to improvise using an experimental NASA navigation payload that had not been certified for primary guidance. *Odysseus* landed but came to rest on its side after one of its legs caught on the surface. NASA confirmed it had received data from its payloads and declared the mission a success. The moment marked the end of a 52-year gap in American lunar landings.

IM-2, carrying the call sign *Athena*, followed in the first quarter of 2025, again on a Nova-C, again to the lunar surface. The mission reached its destination but encountered operational complications analogous to those that characterised IM-1 — a pattern that speaks less to systemic failure than to the brute difficulty of landing on a body with no atmosphere, no GPS, and a surface whose terrain models carry meaningful uncertainty. Intuitive Machines did not claim perfection; it claimed repeatability, which in the context of an emerging commercial market is the more durable proposition.

## CLPS and the milestone-payment machine

The revenue mechanics of the CLPS programme require some unpacking, because they explain a financial profile that can look alarming to investors accustomed to subscription or recurring-revenue models.

NASA does not pay a fixed annual fee for lunar delivery capacity. It awards task orders — discrete contracts, each with its own scope, schedule, and milestone structure — against a programme-level indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity vehicle with a ceiling of [$4.82 billion](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm). Intuitive Machines, along with Astrobotic, Firefly Aerospace, and a small number of other awardees, compete for those task orders. When an order is won, revenue is recognised as milestones are achieved — typically tied to spacecraft delivery, launch readiness, transit, and surface operations events. The result is a quarterly P&L that looks lumpy to the point of illegibility.

| Period | Revenue | Key driver |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| FY2024 | Material concentration | IM-1 *Odysseus* milestone recognition |
| FY2025 full year | $250M–$300M | IM-2 preparation; partial IM-2 recognition |
| Q4 2025 | $44.8M (–18% YoY) | Post-IM-1 recognition trough; IM-2/IM-3 ramp |
| FY2026 guidance | $900M–$1B | Lanteris close + IM-5 task order + continued CLPS awards |

*Sources: [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm); [FY2025 earnings press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000119312525263400/d17822dex991.htm)*

The Q4 2025 revenue decline of 18% year-over-year was, in this context, almost arithmetically inevitable. The IM-1 milestones that had swelled fiscal 2024 revenue were gone; IM-2 had not yet generated equivalent milestone payments; and IM-3 was still in preparation. Gross margin in the quarter was 19%, a figure that reflects early-stage programme economics rather than structural cost problems. The company was burning cash to build the next mission stack, the same pattern that characterised SpaceX's early Commercial Resupply Services years before that programme achieved the density of task orders required to generate consistent earnings.

## Nova-D and the South Pole bet

The IM-5 task order, worth [$180.4 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm) and the largest single CLPS award made to any provider as of the snapshot date, introduces a fundamentally different vehicle into the Intuitive Machines fleet. The Nova-D is a cargo-class lander — significantly larger than the Nova-C, capable of delivering meaningfully greater payload mass to the surface. Where Nova-C targets roughly 100 kilograms of customer payload, Nova-D is designed to deliver the kind of cargo capacity that begins to make infrastructure pre-positioning — fuel depots, surface equipment, habitat components — commercially viable.

IM-5 is tasked with delivering seven science and technology payloads to the Lunar South Pole, a destination of acute strategic interest because of the water-ice deposits in permanently shadowed craters that NASA's Artemis programme intends to exploit for life support and propellant production. The South Pole is also one of the most technically demanding landing destinations on the Moon — terrain is extreme, illumination is intermittent, and communication geometry with Earth requires relay infrastructure that does not yet fully exist. Intuitive Machines' proprietary Lunar TT&C capability, one of the assets sitting inside Lunar Data Services, is directly relevant to navigating that communications architecture.

The Nova-D programme also signals the company's intent to move up the value chain from payload courier toward infrastructure provider. A lander that can carry tonnes of cargo is not merely a bigger taxi; it is a potential logistics platform for the sustained human presence that Artemis is supposed to establish.

## Orbital Services: the engineering spine

Between lunar missions, Intuitive Machines' engineering workforce does not sit idle. The Orbital Services segment captures the broader space-systems work — NASA studies, defence-adjacent engineering contracts, DARPA and Space Force engagements — that generates revenue on timescales measured in quarters rather than mission cycles. This segment is less visible in investor presentations because it lacks the narrative drama of a lunar landing, but it performs a critical function: it keeps the skilled-labour base intact and utilised during the valleys between major CLPS milestone payments.

The segment also serves as a credentialling mechanism. Contracts with the Department of Defense and U.S. Space Force validate Intuitive Machines as a national-security-relevant operator, a designation that matters both for contract eligibility and for the security-clearance infrastructure that opens certain categories of government work. As the company moves toward prime-contractor status, that national-security credentialling becomes a meaningful competitive asset.

## Lanteris and the satellite-systems pivot

The $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems — structured as $450 million in cash and $350 million in stock, with an expected close in the first quarter of 2026 — is the transaction that transforms the business-segment architecture entirely.

Lanteris brings what Intuitive Machines could not organically assemble in any reasonable timeframe: a Boeing-pedigree satellite-systems engineering organisation led by Chris Johnson, who served as President of Boeing Satellite Systems International before joining Lanteris. The acquired company's customer relationships sit in the institutional government and commercial satellite markets — a universe of procurement that operates on contract vehicles, clearances, and programme histories that take decades to accumulate.

The combined backlog of $943 million disclosed post-close reflects both the Lanteris existing programme base and the Intuitive Machines CLPS task-order stack. The CLPS programme's $4.82 billion ceiling with $150 million in near-term guaranteed funding provides the floor; Lanteris's satellite-systems book provides the immediate scale.

Johnson's arrival as President of Lanteris Space Systems within the combined entity also reshapes the management depth at the segment level. Where Intuitive Machines' leadership has historically been concentrated in lunar operations expertise — Steve Altemus ran NASA JSC's engineering directorate before co-founding the company — Lanteris brings institutional prime-contractor experience to a team that previously had to subcontract that capability.

The FY2026 revenue guidance of $900 million to $1 billion, with positive Adjusted EBITDA, is comprehensible only when the acquisition contribution is properly weighted. Organic CLPS revenue, even with IM-5 ramping and continued task-order awards, would not reach that range. The 3x-to-4x implied growth from FY2025 to FY2026 is substantially an acquisition-driven step-change — which is not, in itself, a criticism. The strategic logic is that lunar logistics, in-space communications, satellite systems, and defence-adjacent engineering are more defensible as an integrated capability stack than as four separate subscale businesses. What Intuitive Machines is assembling, one task order and one acquisition at a time, is a vertically integrated space prime — not the legacy model of Lockheed or Boeing, but something purpose-built for the era in which the Moon is becoming an operational environment rather than a destination.

chapters.title: From $300M to $1B revenue in twelve months
chapters.body:
The numbers that defined Intuitive Machines' fiscal year 2025 told two different stories depending on which end of the timeline you stood. Quarterly revenue of $44.8 million in the fourth quarter — an 18 percent decline from the prior-year period — and a gross margin that had only just cleared 19 percent suggested a company still finding its commercial footing. The FY26 guidance of $900 million to $1 billion in revenue, with positive Adjusted EBITDA, pointed toward something categorically different: an operating-profitable space prime with a revenue base three to four times larger than anything the company had previously achieved. The distance between those two data points, compressed into approximately twelve months, represents the most consequential financial transformation in Intuitive Machines' short public history.

Understanding that gap requires unpacking three interlocking forces: the inherent lumpiness of NASA milestone-payment accounting, the weight of an $800 million acquisition closing in the first quarter of 2026, and the compounding effect of a CLPS task-order portfolio now anchored by the largest single award the programme has ever issued.

## The FY25 Baseline: Reading the Lumps

The 18 percent year-over-year decline in Q4 2025 revenue was less a sign of deteriorating business conditions than a function of when NASA recognises contract milestones. Intuitive Machines' first lunar mission — IM-1's *Odysseus* lander, which touched down at the lunar South Pole region on February 22, 2024, making it the first private vehicle in history to land on the Moon — generated revenue recognised across fiscal years 2024 and 2025. By the time the fourth quarter of 2025 arrived, much of the IM-1 milestone stream had been absorbed, and IM-2 and IM-3 were still in preparation rather than final delivery phases. The result was a revenue trough that accurately reflected the accounting cadence of long-duration government space contracts rather than any deterioration in the underlying order book.

Full-year 2025 revenue fell in the range of $250 million to $300 million, according to the company's [FY2025 10-K filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm). That range itself carries a structural caveat: Intuitive Machines' revenue recognition is project-driven, milestone-weighted, and subject to the timing of NASA acceptance events — conditions that make precise year-end figures variable until the filing is complete. What was not in dispute entering 2026 was that the company carried a gross margin structure in the high teens at best, a cost base oriented around mission engineering and spacecraft development, and a balance sheet still absorbing the pre-launch burn of successive lunar programmes.

## The Lanteris Equation: $800 Million for a New Identity

If fiscal year 2025 represented the final chapter of Intuitive Machines as a pure-play lunar delivery specialist, the $800 million acquisition of Lanteris Space Systems — announced before the close of FY25 and completed in the first quarter of 2026 — opened something categorically different.

The transaction structure, comprising [$450 million in cash and $350 million in stock](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000119312525263400/d17822dex991.htm), valued a company that carried Boeing Satellite Systems International's engineering legacy into new ownership. Chris Johnson, Lanteris's chief executive and former president of Boeing Satellite Systems International, became President of Lanteris Space Systems within Intuitive Machines upon close. The addition of that leadership pedigree was not incidental to the strategic rationale: Intuitive Machines was not simply acquiring revenue. It was purchasing the programme management infrastructure, the systems-engineering depth, and the government contracting relationships that distinguish a satellite-systems prime from a mission-delivery specialist — the difference, in the language of Pentagon procurement, between a tier-one integrator and a payload bus operator.

The financial footprint of the deal registered immediately in the backlog. Post-acquisition, total contracted backlog stood at $943 million — a figure that, measured against the company's FY25 revenue range of $250 million to $300 million, represented approximately three years of trailing revenue in contracted work. The $943 million figure reflects both the absorbed Lanteris programme base and the organic CLPS task-order pipeline, making it a composite visibility metric rather than a homogeneous one.

The $450 million cash component of the acquisition is a material balance-sheet event by any measure. The precise financing terms — whether funded from existing cash reserves, new debt facilities, or some combination of the two — were not fully disaggregated in available summary filings at the time of this snapshot. That specificity matters for assessing the post-close capital structure and the leverage profile the company will service as it executes the FY26 revenue ramp. Investors should consult the full acquisition 8-K and subsequent 10-Q disclosures for complete balance-sheet transparency.

## Decomposing the FY26 Ramp

The path from $250–300 million to $900 million–$1 billion in revenue is not a single mechanism. It is an overlay of three distinct revenue streams, each with different certainty gradients and different recognition timings.

| Revenue driver | Nature of contribution | Certainty basis |
|---|---|---|
| Lanteris consolidation (~9 months in FY26 P&L) | Largest single contributor to FY26 step-up | Acquisition closed Q1 2026; contracted legacy backlog |
| CLPS organic task-order ramp (IM-3, IM-4, IM-5) | Material organic contribution | Task orders awarded; milestone schedule-dependent |
| IM-5 task order alone ($180.4M, Nova-D, Lunar South Pole) | Single largest CLPS task order issued to date | Contracted; execution risk on delivery timeline |

Because the Lanteris acquisition closed during the first quarter of 2026, roughly nine months of consolidated Lanteris revenue flow through the combined income statement in FY26. That consolidation effect — not organic growth — is the primary mathematical driver of the 3-to-4 times revenue expansion. Management guidance has been explicit that FY26 projections incorporate this consolidation, and sophisticated readers of the eventual FY26 10-K will find that the organic-versus-acquired revenue disaggregation is the most important analytical cut for evaluating whether the underlying lunar business is scaling on its own terms.

The organic CLPS contribution nonetheless carries independent significance. The IM-5 task order, at $180.4 million, is the largest single award the CLPS programme has ever issued. It funds delivery of scientific and exploration payloads to the Lunar South Pole aboard the larger cargo-class Nova-D lander — a vehicle designed to carry substantially greater mass to the surface than the Nova-C class that flew IM-1 and IM-2. The progression from Nova-C to Nova-D is itself a programme-maturity signal: NASA is committing larger dollar values to individual deliveries as institutional confidence in the commercial lunar logistics model compounds across successful missions.

## NASA CLPS: The Ceiling and the Floor

The $4.82 billion contract ceiling on the NASA CLPS vehicle is the structural parameter that most shapes long-run revenue expectations. Ceilings on indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contracts do not represent guaranteed revenue — they represent the maximum the government can obligate under the vehicle without re-competing. The relevant near-term floor is $150 million in guaranteed funding, the portion NASA committed regardless of task-order award activity.

The practical arithmetic between ceiling and floor defines the investment proposition's risk distribution. At current task-order sizing — with IM-5 alone at $180.4 million — a handful of awards can move the organic revenue needle materially. But task orders are episodic, subject to NASA budget cycles and programme priorities, and contingent on Intuitive Machines' continued mission performance. The IM-1 *Odysseus* landing, despite its operational complications upon touchdown, was counted by NASA and by the company as a mission success sufficient to justify continued CLPS investment. IM-2's *Athena* lander, which reached the lunar surface in the first quarter of 2025, extended that track record. Each successful surface delivery strengthens the basis for subsequent task-order awards at increasing scale.

## The Operating-Profitability Inflection

Until FY26, Intuitive Machines operated as a cash-consuming development organisation — a pattern common to companies building first-of-kind space infrastructure against fixed-price government contracts before the revenue base reaches scale. The guidance for positive Adjusted EBITDA in FY26 marks the end of that phase, at least on the adjusted metric.

The mechanism is operating leverage. Intuitive Machines carries a fixed engineering and programme management cost base built to support lunar mission operations, spacecraft development, and government contracting infrastructure. As Lanteris revenue consolidates and CLPS task orders ramp through the year, that fixed base spreads across a substantially larger revenue denominator. The gross margin trajectory — still at 19 percent in Q4 2025 — should expand as higher-margin satellite-systems programmes from the Lanteris portfolio contribute to the blended company mix, though the precise margin profile of the acquired business was not separately detailed in available summary filings at the time of this snapshot.

Adjusted EBITDA is, it is worth stating plainly, a non-GAAP measure. The distance between Adjusted EBITDA and GAAP operating income will be shaped by stock-based compensation, depreciation of mission hardware and development assets, and any acquisition-related charges from the Lanteris purchase price allocation. Investors accustomed to GAAP profitability as the relevant threshold should treat the FY26 Adjusted EBITDA guidance as the beginning of a journey toward GAAP operating profitability rather than its destination. Compensation structure and executive pay against the revenue ramp — a proxy-disclosure question that often surfaces when a small-cap growth company crosses the threshold into operating profitability — was not separately detailed in available DEF 14A summary at this snapshot and merits direct review of the proxy filing.

## What the Trajectory Signals

At the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, Intuitive Machines had completed the Lanteris acquisition and was executing against a guidance range that, if achieved, would represent one of the fastest revenue ramps in the commercial space sector's recent history. The $943 million total backlog provided contractual visibility through a meaningful portion of the forecast period. The $4.82 billion CLPS ceiling provided structural context for long-duration revenue potential, while the $150 million in guaranteed near-term funding anchored the downside.

The open questions — how acquisition financing reshapes the capital structure, how blended gross margin evolves as Lanteris programmes mature, and whether GAAP profitability follows Adjusted EBITDA with reasonable lag — represent the analytical work that remains. What is already established is the inflection point itself: a company founded out of a NASA engineering office, first to land a private vehicle on the Moon, had by the spring of 2026 constructed the financial architecture of an operating-profitable space prime. The transition from cash-burning venture to industrialised lunar logistics operator, measured in revenue multiples across a single fiscal year, is the central fact of Intuitive Machines' investment story entering its next chapter.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Pre-EBITDA Story With Post-Acquisition Scale

Valuing Intuitive Machines requires holding two contradictions simultaneously. The company is the only private entity to have soft-landed on the Moon — twice — and yet it has never reported positive EBITDA, its quarterly revenue has ranged between $28 million and $44.8 million in recent reported periods, and its FY26 transformation thesis rests almost entirely on the successful integration of an $800 million acquisition that closed in Q1 2026. Standard multiples built for mature industrials or high-growth software do not travel cleanly to this sector. The primary analytical lens is EV/Revenue, with a secondary watch on EV/Backlog. Trailing price-to-earnings is inapplicable; forward P/E is speculative given that adjusted EBITDA positivity — itself a target rather than a demonstrated outcome — would represent only a thin margin on the FY26 revenue base. Price-to-book offers limited signal in an asset-light government-contracting model whose key assets are programme certifications, mission heritage, and NASA programme relationships rather than tangible plant.

## Current Multiples and Market Cap Reasoning

As of the frozen snapshot date of 2026-05-23, Intuitive Machines had not published a precise post-Lanteris share count in the most recently available public filings reviewed for this dossier. Working from disclosed data: the company carried approximately 80–85 million shares outstanding prior to the Lanteris stock consideration of $350 million. Depending on the negotiated issuance price — typically a volume-weighted average over a defined look-back window — the stock tranche would have added approximately 25–40 million shares, implying a post-close diluted share base in the range of 110–125 million shares. Against a price range of $12–16 per share — consistent with the range observed in the months surrounding the Lanteris close — the equity market capitalisation sits approximately $1.3 billion to $2.0 billion.

Net debt introduces further estimation. The $450 million cash portion of the Lanteris consideration ([Intuitive Machines 8-K / press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000119312525263400/d17822dex991.htm)), layered onto what was already a cash-consuming pre-profitability balance sheet, implies that Intuitive Machines entered FY26 carrying meaningful incremental debt or completed a secondary equity offering to fund the transaction. A working assumption of $300–450 million in net debt post-close places enterprise value in the range of $1.6 billion to $2.4 billion. Against the FY26 revenue guide of $900 million to $1 billion (midpoint $950 million), the implied forward EV/Revenue multiple falls approximately 1.7x–2.5x.

On a backlog basis — arguably the more instructive measure given NASA's milestone-based revenue recognition cadence — the $943 million total backlog post-Lanteris ([FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026027026/lunr-20251231annualreportf.pdf)) implies an EV/Backlog ratio broadly in line with EV/Revenue, since the backlog represents roughly one year of conversion at the guided pace.

## Historical Multiple Context: From Speculative Premium to Execution Discount

Intuitive Machines came to market via de-SPAC in February 2023 during a period of sharp contraction in space-sector equities. The stock initially carried a speculative premium as investors priced the optionality of the first private Moon landing against a venture-scale operating profile. That premium compressed through 2023 as cash burn and revenue lumpiness became visible in quarterly filings.

The IM-1 Odysseus landing on February 22, 2024 — the first successful private soft landing in history — triggered a meaningful re-rating. The market assigned incremental probability to the company's core thesis: that repeatable lunar logistics was an achievable commercial business rather than an aspirational concept. IM-2's operational complications during Q1 2025 reasserted an execution-risk discount, partially reversing those gains.

The Lanteris acquisition announcement effectively repriced the company's identity. No longer purely a lunar-lander startup, Intuitive Machines had recruited Boeing-grade satellite systems capability via Chris Johnson, who had served as President of Boeing Satellite Systems International before leading Lanteris. The multiple at which LUNR has traded since reflects an ongoing negotiation between the scale premium warranted by the FY26 revenue trajectory and the integration discount warranted by the complexity of merging two distinct space businesses within a single fiscal year.

## Peer Multiple Comparison

The relevant peer universe spans government-prime space systems companies and commercial space operators, none of which offer a perfect analogue to LUNR's current stage and business mix.

| Company | Ticker | FY26E Revenue (est.) | Approx. EV | EV / FY26E Rev | Key differentiator |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Intuitive Machines** | LUNR | ~$950M midpoint | ~$1.8–2.4B | ~1.9–2.5x | Lunar prime + Lanteris integration year |
| Rocket Lab | RKLB | ~$700–800M | ~$8–10B | ~11–13x | Proven launch cadence; Neutron optionality |
| Redwire Corp | RDW | ~$300–350M | ~$550–750M | ~1.7–2.2x | Space manufacturing; ISS-adjacent |
| Planet Labs | PL | ~$280–310M | ~$500–700M | ~1.7–2.3x | Earth observation; recurring data model |
| Kratos Defense | KTOS | ~$1.1–1.2B | ~$3.5–4.0B | ~3.0–3.5x | Defence-prime posture; EBITDA margin track record |
| Terran Orbital | LLAP | Acquired | N/A | N/A | Removed from public peer set; Lockheed deal |

The most instructive comparison is Rocket Lab. RKLB commands a significant multiple premium — estimated at 11–13x forward EV/Revenue — that reflects a proven launch cadence, consistent execution across dozens of Electron missions, and space systems revenue from the Sinclair and SatRev acquisitions. LUNR's discount to RKLB is defensible on execution-track-record grounds alone: both IM-1 and IM-2 reached the lunar surface but with operational anomalies that constrained mission deliverables. However, LUNR's FY26 revenue at $950M midpoint is materially larger than RKLB's, and its government-contracting backlog provides a degree of revenue visibility that Rocket Lab's commercial launch manifest does not.

Kratos provides a different reference point: a mature defence-adjacent space and unmanned systems business with consistent EBITDA margins and a proven prime-contracting posture. LUNR trading broadly in line with Kratos on EV/Revenue is noteworthy given LUNR's earlier stage of profitability — the comparison flatters LUNR only if FY26 EBITDA inflection is achieved and sustained.

## What the Current Price Implies

Backing out from a ~2x EV/FY26 Revenue multiple, the market appears to be pricing: successful Lanteris integration producing full consolidated revenue contribution; continued CLPS task-order awards at historical cadence; and initial adjusted EBITDA positivity at low single-digit margins. What is evidently *not* priced at current levels: meaningful margin expansion beyond the initial positive-territory threshold, acceleration of CLPS task-order awards toward the $4.82 billion contract ceiling ([FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026027026/lunr-20251231annualreportf.pdf)), or a second lunar programme beyond the existing NASA mandate.

The implicit DCF embedded in a ~2x forward revenue multiple for a company guiding toward positive EBITDA and 3–4x revenue growth suggests the market is applying a high discount rate — consistent with a blended perception of execution risk, integration risk, and the programme-level concentration risk inherent in a business where a single NASA task-order delay or mission anomaly can move a quarter's revenue materially. The IM-5 task order at $180.4 million represents the largest single CLPS task order awarded to date; successful execution on the Nova-D cargo-class lander would be a material de-risking event for subsequent multiple expansion.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $28–35 per share.** Lanteris integration proceeds on schedule, with run-rate synergies materialising in FY27. The IM-5 Nova-D mission executes cleanly, establishing the cargo-class lander programme and accelerating follow-on task-order awards. FY26 adjusted EBITDA margin reaches 5–8%, establishing a credible path toward double-digit margins. A second customer — an international space agency or a commercial lunar-economy participant — awards an incremental contract outside the CLPS vehicle. The market re-rates to 3.5–4x EV/FY27 revenue of approximately $1.2–1.4 billion, implying an enterprise value of $4.2–5.6 billion and a share price in the $28–35 range after accounting for post-Lanteris diluted share count and net debt.

**Base case — $15–20 per share.** Lanteris integration takes twelve to eighteen months to fully consolidate, with FY26 revenue tracking toward the midpoint of the $900M–$1B guide. Adjusted EBITDA turns positive in FY26 but remains below 5%. NASA CLPS task-order cadence continues at current pace without acceleration. The multiple stays rangebound at 1.8–2.2x forward revenue as the market awaits margin evidence through FY27. Share price trades in the $15–20 range as FY27 estimates firm and integration execution becomes verifiable.

**Bear case — $6–9 per share.** Integration costs from Lanteris prove higher than guided, with FY26 revenue tracking at or below the $900M floor and adjusted EBITDA positivity delayed to FY27. A mission complication in IM-3 or IM-5 generates programme-level scrutiny at NASA and introduces a risk of task-order cadence disruption. The stock de-rates to 1.0–1.3x forward revenue — consistent with distressed or uncertain government contractors — implying a share price of $6–9. This scenario is not a tail case: the company has delivered two missions with meaningful operational anomalies in succession, and the Lanteris business — a satellite-systems integrator being absorbed by a lunar-lander startup — carries inherent cultural and operational integration risk.

## The Consensus Gap

The dossier's read diverges from an implied consensus in one specific respect. The consensus narrative treats the $900M–$1B FY26 revenue guide primarily as a Lanteris contribution story — which it largely is — and discounts the guide proportionally to integration execution risk. What consensus appears to underweight is the structural significance of NASA's procurement posture embedded in the CLPS contract ceiling. At $4.82 billion authorised across multiple award periods, with the first task orders barely scratching the surface, the ceiling represents a revenue roadmap extending well beyond FY26. If NASA treats South Pole logistics as a sustained multi-year infrastructure programme rather than a sequence of one-off milestone contracts — a framing consistent with the Artemis programme's stated ambitions — the ceiling becomes the most important number in any LUNR valuation exercise. The gap between the current multiple and the Rocket Lab premium exists precisely because that ceiling has not yet been converted into committed task orders at scale. The rate at which it converts is, ultimately, the rate at which LUNR's valuation gap closes.

chapters.title: From IM-1 milestone to FY26 inflection guide
chapters.body:
## A Blank-Cheque Beginning

When Intuitive Machines completed its merger with Inflection Point Acquisition Corp. in February 2023 and began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker LUNR, the market was buying something unusual: a company with a handful of NASA contracts, a lander prototype, and a thesis — that the United States government's return to the Moon would be executed, in part, by a twelve-year-old Houston startup staffed by former NASA engineers.

The financial profile at listing was characteristically pre-scale for a SPAC target. Revenue was a series of NASA cost-plus and milestone-based contract payments; the company had not yet flown a mission, and the milestone-payment recognition model meant that most of the financial story would be written later. The institutional anchor was the CLPS programme relationship — a framework that gave Intuitive Machines a procurement channel but not a guaranteed income stream. What the de-SPAC actually delivered was a public balance sheet to fund the Nova-C lander programme through to mission execution and a liquid stock currency that would eventually fund the Lanteris transaction. Michael Blitzer's Inflection Point sponsored the vehicle and joined the board; his Kingstown Capital roots brought a shareholder-activist sensibility to a board that otherwise skewed deeply toward government-and-defence credentials.

## The 2023 Revenue Print: Promising, Lumpy, Inconclusive

Through 2023, Intuitive Machines delivered the kind of quarterly revenue prints that characterise NASA milestone-based operators: modest, irregular, and resistant to extrapolation. The company was in mission-preparation mode for IM-1 — procuring payloads, integrating customer instruments, and completing lander acceptance testing. Revenue recognition followed programme milestones rather than time elapsed, which produced an uneven cadence that frustrated any attempt to construct a clean run-rate model.

The CLPS framework — under which NASA effectively purchases delivery services rather than specifying hardware — meant that revenue arrived in tranches: at contract award, at integration milestones, and, critically, at mission completion. For a company flying its first mission, the latter category was still theoretical in 2023.

## February 22, 2024: The Malapert Moment

The quarter that changed everything was Q1 2024. On February 15, 2024, Intuitive Machines launched the Nova-C lander 'Odysseus' — mission designation IM-1 — aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Kennedy Space Center. Seven days later, on [February 22](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm), Odysseus touched down near the Malapert A crater at the lunar south pole, becoming the first privately-built spacecraft to soft-land on the Moon and the first American-built spacecraft to do so since Apollo 17 in December 1972.

The stock reaction was sharp and immediate. LUNR shares surged as the landing was confirmed, the price move reflecting not just mission success but the repricing of a binary risk: until that moment, a lunar landing by a private operator was an unproven proposition. Post-landing, Intuitive Machines held a demonstrated capability that no other private entity could claim.

The operational complications were disclosed promptly. A landing-leg failure caused Odysseus to come to rest on its side, partially obscuring solar panels and compressing the operational mission window. Despite the anomaly, IM-1 transmitted data and Intuitive Machines was able to claim milestone completion, triggering the associated revenue recognition. Altemus characterised the mission as a historic achievement even in its imperfect form — the landing itself was the proof point the programme required.

## FY24: The First Mission-Era Print

The FY24 full-year results reflected IM-1 revenue recognition flowing through the income statement. The milestone-payment model meant that revenue associated with IM-1 was recognised partly in the year of mission execution, creating a substantially larger FY24 revenue figure relative to the pre-mission 2023 baseline. Gross margins remained challenged, reflecting the early-stage cost structure of a company that had never built and flown a production lander at scale before.

The stock-volatility pattern that would define LUNR's trading character was established in this period: sharp spikes around mission events, followed by consolidation as investors processed the underlying operating-profitability trajectory. Revenue was real; sustained profitability was deferred.

## IM-2 'Athena' and the FY25 Cadence

The IM-2 mission — 'Athena' — launched in early 2025 carrying a complement of NASA science instruments and commercial cargo. The lander reached the lunar surface in Q1 2025, repeating both the achievement and the complications of its predecessor: Athena touched down but encountered operational difficulties on the surface. The pattern reinforced a consistent observation: Intuitive Machines could reliably deliver hardware to the Moon, but the precision of surface operations at the class of the Nova-C lander remained technically demanding.

For the FY25 financial cadence, the IM-2 mission was the primary revenue-generation event of the first half. But the year's quarterly progression illustrated the structural feature that defines milestone-payment operators: [Q4 2025 revenue of $44.8 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000119312525263400/d17822dex991.htm) — down approximately 18 per cent year-on-year — was not a signal of deteriorating commercial momentum. It was the arithmetic of a company that had already recognised the bulk of its deliverable revenue from in-flight programmes, and whose next large recognition event resided in missions still in preparation.

| Period | Revenue | Gross Margin | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025 (full year) | $250M–$300M | — | Lumpy milestone recognition; IM-2 primary event |
| Q4 2025 | $44.8M | 19% | −18% YoY; post-IM-2 inter-mission trough |
| FY2026E (guidance) | $900M–$1B | — | ~3–4× growth; Lanteris contribution + CLPS ramp |

Peter McGrath, who had joined as CFO in September 2024 following a 31-year Boeing career spanning structural analysis, Phantom Works, and launch services, was explicit with investors about the recognition dynamic. The FY25 full-year range of $250–$300 million represented genuine commercial traction — a company that had executed two lunar missions and collected milestone payments from NASA and commercial customers — but the quarterly lumpiness required investors to think in mission cycles rather than calendar quarters. The 19 per cent gross margin in Q4 2025, while thin, marked a progression from the near-zero margins of the pre-mission period and confirmed that the delivery model, imperfect as it was operationally, was generating economics above cost of revenue.

## Lanteris: The Structural Bet

Against this backdrop, the Lanteris Space Systems acquisition — announced ahead of the FY25 full-year print — was the most consequential event in Intuitive Machines' post-SPAC history. The [$800 million transaction](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026027026/lunr-20251231annualreportf.pdf) ($450 million cash, $350 million stock) brought Boeing Satellite Systems-grade engineering capability into a company that had, until that moment, been a single-product lunar-delivery operator.

Chris Johnson — who had led Lanteris and before that served as President of Boeing Satellite Systems International for more than two decades — was named President of Lanteris Space Systems within Intuitive Machines, effective January 2026. The board rationale was unambiguous: the Lanteris product line extended the addressable market from lunar surface delivery into satellite manufacturing and broader space systems, the portfolio of a prime contractor rather than a mission-logistics specialist.

The structural consequence for backlog was equally clear. Total backlog post-Lanteris stood at $943 million. The NASA CLPS contract ceiling had been expanded to $4.82 billion, with $150 million guaranteed near-term. The IM-5 task order — $180.4 million, the largest single CLPS task order awarded to date — directed seven science and technology payloads to the Lunar South Pole aboard the larger cargo-class Nova-D lander, a material step up from the Nova-C flown on IM-1 and IM-2, signalling both NASA's confidence in the platform and its intent to use Intuitive Machines for progressively more complex surface operations.

## The FY26 Inflection: What $900M Actually Means

The FY26 guidance of $900 million to $1 billion in revenue — implying approximately 3–4 times FY25 — is not primarily an organic growth story. It is an acquisition story with an organic underlayer. The Lanteris contribution, once the Q1 2026 close completed, added a recurring revenue base in satellite systems that the legacy lunar-delivery business could not have generated independently on that timeline. The CLPS task-order ramp — including IM-3, IM-4, and the IM-5 Nova-D mission — provided the organic component.

The critical marker embedded in the guidance is the Adjusted EBITDA target: positive. Since the de-SPAC in February 2023, Intuitive Machines had been a cash-consuming organisation — funding lander development, mission execution, and acquisition integration. The FY26 positive Adjusted EBITDA target is the company's first commitment to operating-level profitability and the signal that management believes the combined entity is crossing from venture-scale capital consumption to self-sustaining commercial operation.

The path to that inflection requires Lanteris integration to proceed without material cost overruns, CLPS task orders to be awarded and executed on schedule, and NASA's Artemis programme to sustain the political and budgetary support that underpins the entire commercial lunar economy. Each condition carries execution risk. What Intuitive Machines had established by May 2026, across three years of post-SPAC life, was that the foundational technical risk — the question of whether a private operator could land on the Moon — had been answered twice over. The financial risk of converting that capability into a profitable space-prime business remained the open question as the company entered the most consequential fiscal year of its short public history.

chapters.title: NASA JSC, Sony, Space Force, and Kingstown Capital
chapters.body:
## The Founding Engineers

When Stephen Altemus left the Johnson Space Center in 2013 to co-found Intuitive Machines, he carried with him something rarer than a government pension: institutional credibility earned in the worst circumstances American aerospace has known. On the morning of February 1, 2003, the Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry, killing all seven crew members. Altemus, then a senior engineer at JSC, was named Columbia Reconstruction Director — the person responsible for coordinating the physical and technical reconstruction of what the accident investigation board needed to understand the failure. It was among the most disciplined aerospace engineering management assignments in modern spaceflight history, a role demanding forensic rigor, interagency coordination, and the kind of institutional credibility that cannot be conferred by rank alone.

That credential preceded a tenure as JSC's Director of Engineering and eventually Deputy Director, the second-highest operational role at the centre that manages human spaceflight from mission control. Altemus, 62, holds a B.S. in Aeronautical Engineering from Embry Riddle Aeronautical University and an M.S. in Engineering Management from the University of Central Florida. He joined NASA in 1989 at Kennedy Space Center on the Space Shuttle Program. By the time he departed to co-found Intuitive Machines, he had spent twenty-four years inside the institutional infrastructure of American human spaceflight.

His co-founder brought a different kind of pedigree. Dr. Kamal Ghaffarian, 67, is the chairman of Intuitive Machines and one of the most prolific deep-tech founder-chairman figures of his generation. His academic formation — two undergraduate degrees, a master's in information management, and two doctorates in management information systems and technology — is the unusual product of someone who understood early that the bureaucratic and technical dimensions of aerospace contracting were inseparable. He built Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies from a services contractor into a firm substantial enough to attract KBR's acquisition in 2018. Since then, his portfolio of founder-chairman positions has expanded to include Axiom Space, the private orbital module operator; X Energy, the advanced nuclear reactor developer; Quantum Space, the cislunar intelligence startup; and PTX, among others. His chairmanship of Intuitive Machines is the institutional anchor that positions a co-founded startup to operate alongside companies with decades of government contracting history.

## A Board Configured for This Moment

The six-director board Altemus and Ghaffarian assembled is unusually calibrated for the specific phase of the business. As of May 2026, Intuitive Machines was executing the integration of its $800 million Lanteris Space Systems acquisition, managing a $4.82 billion NASA CLPS contract ceiling, and guiding a revenue ramp from the $250–300 million FY2025 range toward a $900 million–$1 billion FY2026 outlook. The board composition — national security, aerospace finance, corporate governance, and financial engineering — maps directly onto those four execution risks.

William J. Liquori, 57, is the Class I director providing the national security anchor. A retired Lieutenant General in the U.S. Space Force, Liquori served as Chief Strategy and Resourcing Officer — the officer responsible for budget architecture and long-range planning across the newest military branch. His B.A. in Computer Science from Boston University was followed by three graduate degrees: an M.S. in Computer Resources and Information Management from Webster University, and advanced military education at Air University (Airpower Art and Science) and Marine Corps University (Strategic Studies). He chairs the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee and the Conflicts Committee, and holds board seats at True Anomaly, the space situational awareness venture, and the Space Force Association. In the context of a company whose addressable market includes Space Force and Department of Defense infrastructure on and near the Moon, Liquori's institutional relationships are not incidental to the directorship — they are the point of it.

Robert L. Masson, 57, occupies the audit and aerospace finance seat. A 1992 Naval Academy graduate in economics who subsequently earned an MBA from Harvard Business School, Masson flew as a Naval Aviator until 2001 before transitioning to a career as a chief financial officer in defense and industrial manufacturing — Raytheon Technologies, Flowserve, Hypertherm, and Latham Group. He chairs the Audit Committee and sits on the Compensation, Nominating and Corporate Governance, Conflicts, and Strategic Transactions committees. He also chairs the audit committee at Tech-Etch, a precision-components manufacturer with defense applications. The Naval Academy + Harvard MBA + Raytheon + Naval Aviator pedigree is the precise credential profile for an audit committee chair overseeing NASA fixed-price contract accounting and the financial complexity of absorbing a satellite-systems business.

## The Financial Engineer and the Governance Architect

Michael Blitzer, 48, is the Class II director who is simultaneously the financial memory of LUNR's capital structure and its most active dealmaker. Blitzer founded Kingstown Capital Management in 2006, building it into a multi-billion-dollar asset manager serving endowments and foundations, before transitioning to chair Inflection Point Asset Management in 2024. The prior Inflection Point Acquisition Corp SPAC was the vehicle that took Intuitive Machines public via de-SPAC in February 2023. Blitzer holds a B.S. from Cornell and an MBA from Columbia Business School, where he also spent five years as an investing instructor. His institutional formation included Gotham Asset Management, the Joel Greenblatt-founded value fund, and an early career at J.P. Morgan Securities advising on private debt and capital raises.

By May 2026, his concurrent board roles made him the highest-frequency public-company capital-markets dealmaker on the board: Chairman of USA Rare Earth (Nasdaq: USAR) since its 2025 listing; Lead Independent Director at Merlin Labs (Nasdaq: MRLN); and active SPAC sponsorship through Inflection Point Acquisition Corps III and V. At Intuitive Machines, he chairs the Compensation Committee and the Strategic Transactions Committee — the body that approved the $800 million Lanteris acquisition. No director on the board was better positioned to evaluate whether that transaction's structure served shareholder interests.

Nicole Seligman, 69, rounds out the Class II directors and represents the most credentialed corporate-governance appointment on any U.S. listed company at LUNR's market capitalisation. She graduated magna cum laude from Harvard College and magna cum laude from Harvard Law School, clerked for Justice Thurgood Marshall at the U.S. Supreme Court, practised as a litigation partner at Williams & Connolly, and then spent a decade inside Sony Corporation, rising from Executive Vice President and Global General Counsel (2005–2014) to President of Sony Corporation of America (2012–2016) and President of Sony Entertainment (2014–2016). The Sony tenure involved managing legal, regulatory, and reputational risk for a Japanese conglomerate navigating U.S. regulatory frameworks across media, technology, and consumer electronics — experience that translates directly into the cross-jurisdictional complexity of a NASA-prime space systems company.

Her subsequent board appointments are the signal. She serves on the board of OpenAI — one of the small group of directors providing fiduciary oversight at arguably the most consequential technology company of the current decade. She also sits on the board of Meira GTx Holdings and Praetorian Acquisition Corp. At Intuitive Machines, she sits on the Audit, Nominating and Corporate Governance, and Conflicts committees. The Seligman appointment in June 2023 — four months after the de-SPAC listing — was a deliberate governance upgrade, signalling to institutional investors that the board understood the fiduciary obligations of a public NASA contractor.

## The Operators

Below the board, the executive team was substantially rebuilt around the Lanteris acquisition. Dr. Timothy Crain, 53, co-founded Intuitive Machines alongside Altemus and Ghaffarian and has served as Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer since February 2026. His PhD in Aerospace Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin preceded a NASA career at JSC that included navigation work on the Mars Science Lander and guidance, navigation, and control development for the Orion spacecraft. Crain is the engineering continuity of the company — the person whose institutional knowledge of the IM lander architecture extends back to the earliest design decisions of the program.

Peter McGrath, 58, joined as Chief Financial Officer in September 2024, arriving from a 31-year career at Boeing that covered structural analysis, Phantom Works advanced development, and launch services. He holds a B.S. and M.S. in Aerospace Engineering alongside an MBA. McGrath's background is precisely the profile that NASA's fixed-price CLPS contracting structure requires on the financial side: someone who understands the engineering economics of aerospace hardware well enough to model cost-to-complete with credibility.

Anna Jones, 47, became Senior Vice President, Chief Legal Officer, and Corporate Secretary in February 2026, the same month Crain's CTO appointment took effect. A J.D. graduate of Northwestern University School of Law, she had previously served as VP Securities and Corporate Counsel at Paysafe and held legal roles at Marathon Oil, ConocoPhillips, and Latham & Watkins. Her appointment as the company's first standalone CLO — rather than relying on outside counsel at the board-secretary level — reflected the legal complexity of managing a $4.82 billion NASA contract ceiling, an $800 million M&A integration, and the ongoing SEC reporting obligations of a post-de-SPAC listed company.

Chris Johnson, 49, is perhaps the acquisition's most tangible human asset. As the former CEO of Lanteris Space Systems and, before that, President of Boeing Satellite Systems International, Johnson brought the institutional manufacturing and systems-engineering capability that Intuitive Machines was buying when it agreed to pay $800 million for Lanteris. He earned a B.S. in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Kansas, an M.S. in Systems Architecting and Engineering from USC, and an MBA from USC, before spending more than two decades at Boeing in defence and commercial satellite roles. His appointment as President of Lanteris Space Systems in January 2026 — immediately upon the acquisition's close — placed him in operational control of the subsidiary that was expected to account for the majority of the revenue jump from the $250–300 million FY2025 range to the $900 million–$1 billion FY2026 outlook.

## The Architecture of the Bench

Taken together, the ten-person governance and executive structure Intuitive Machines assembled by May 2026 was configured for a specific inflection: the moment a lunar-logistics specialist becomes a space systems prime. Altemus and Crain carried the NASA engineering pedigree. Ghaffarian provided the institutional relationships and the founder's tolerance for the time horizons that deep-tech infrastructure requires. Liquori mapped the board to Pentagon and Space Force procurement relationships. Masson brought the aerospace-finance discipline to oversee NASA contract accounting. Blitzer provided the capital-markets architecture and the memory of the original public transaction. Seligman brought the governance credibility — and the OpenAI board seat — that institutional investors scrutinise when deciding whether a small-cap space company is ready for sustained ownership.

What the board notably lacked was a peer-CEO from the operating space industry — no equivalent of Tory Bruno or a sitting large-cap aerospace chief executive. That gap was deliberate: the board's job through the Lanteris integration and early CLPS task-order execution was governance and oversight, not operational second-guessing. The operators — Crain, McGrath, Jones, and Johnson — had been specifically recruited to execute. The board had been assembled to make sure the execution stayed within the bounds of what shareholders, NASA, and the Space Force would collectively tolerate.

chapters.title: NASA, CLPS, and the satellite-systems counterparty addition
chapters.body:
## A contract ceiling and a crowded pool

When NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme was structured in the late 2010s, the agency borrowed deliberately from its own playbook. Like the Commercial Resupply Services contracts that underwrote SpaceX's early Falcon 9 cadence, and the Commercial Crew programme that eventually put American astronauts back on an American rocket, CLPS was designed to spread risk across a pool of pre-qualified vendors, award task orders mission by mission, and let competition drive cost down over time. The total programme ceiling was set at $4.82 billion — a number large enough to sustain a commercial ecosystem across the Artemis decade, yet structured so that no single awardee could treat it as a guaranteed revenue stream. Intuitive Machines entered that pool as one of a handful of companies, won the first operational lunar surface delivery, and has since accumulated more task-order value than any competitor in the programme.

The $4.82 billion ceiling is best understood as an addressable opportunity, not a committed backlog. NASA guarantees only a fraction of the pool's value in near-term awards — roughly $150 million of near-term committed value was disclosed in the company's annual filings — and task orders are competed among the awardees. That structure keeps NASA's cost discipline intact while giving the commercial awardees a reason to invest in launch cadence, reliability, and lunar surface engineering. For Intuitive Machines, the most consequential single task order awarded to date was the $180.4 million IM-5 contract, which calls for the delivery of seven science and technology payloads to the Lunar South Pole aboard the cargo-class Nova-D lander — a platform one size larger than the Nova-C vehicles that carried the first two missions. [SEC 10-K, LUNR FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm)

## The mission catalog: two landings, three more in the pipeline

The operational record begins on 22 February 2024, when the IM-1 lander — call sign *Odysseus*, a Nova-C class vehicle launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 — touched down in the Malapert A crater region near the lunar south pole. The landing was not clean. A sensor switch left in the wrong position during launch preparation disabled the vehicle's primary laser rangefinders; engineers improvised a fix using an experimental NASA instrument on board, and *Odysseus* reached the surface but came to rest on its side, a landing-leg having snagged on the terrain. Despite the orientation, several payloads operated. The company had done what no private enterprise had ever done: it landed a spacecraft on the Moon.

IM-2, the *Athena* mission, followed in the first quarter of 2025 — again a Nova-C class lander, again reaching the lunar surface with operational complications. The pattern of two missions that technically achieved surface contact but encountered engineering difficulties is the acknowledged vulnerability in the investment thesis: the company is still learning, in the most unforgiving environment a vehicle can encounter, and the learning carries real cost. As of the 23 May 2026 snapshot, IM-3 was in active preparation and IM-4 in planning, with the Nova-D-class IM-5 mission — the largest and most complex in the catalogue — carrying the $180.4 million task order and representing the programme's first step toward genuine cargo delivery at scale.

The mission sequence matters for revenue recognition as much as for operational credibility. NASA milestone payments are recognised against task-order completion milestones, producing a revenue profile that looks lumpy to anyone accustomed to a stable SaaS or defence-services contract. The company's fourth-quarter 2025 revenue of $44.8 million was down roughly 18 percent year-on-year, reflecting the reality that IM-1 mission revenue had been substantially recognised in FY2024 and FY2025 was a period of mission preparation rather than delivery. Full-year FY2025 revenue fell in the $250 million to $300 million range. The cadence of task-order awards and the pace of mission execution will govern whether the FY2026 outlook of $900 million to $1 billion in revenue proves achievable on the lunar-delivery side of the ledger.

## Secondary customers and national-security adjacency

Beyond CLPS, Intuitive Machines has cultivated relationships with the national-security customer base that shares an interest in cislunar domain awareness. The Department of Defense, DARPA, and the US Space Force have each engaged the company as a counterparty — the rationale converging on the observation that the same telemetry, tracking, and control capability required for lunar surface operations is exactly what the defence establishment needs to understand the cislunar environment that great-power competition is beginning to contest.

The company's proprietary lunar telemetry, tracking, and control infrastructure — built to support its own missions — represents a potential separate revenue line for government customers who need coverage in cislunar space but lack the assets to provide it themselves.
